hook: One food has never spoiled in 3,000 years. Ever.

scenes.line: Archaeologists cracked open Egyptian tombs and found jars of honey.
scenes.visual_prompt: Stone sarcophagus interior, golden light filtering across dusty ancient pottery vessels, hieroglyphics barely visible on ceramic jars

scenes.line: These jars had been sealed since the pharaohs ruled Egypt.
scenes.visual_prompt: Overhead shot of weathered clay vessels with wax seals intact, surrounded by sand and stone, sunlight casting long shadows

scenes.line: Scientists tasted it. The honey was completely fresh. Perfectly edible.
scenes.visual_prompt: Close-up of golden amber honey being spooned, light refracting through the translucent liquid, viscous and glistening

scenes.line: Your yogurt expires in three weeks. This honey has survived empires.
scenes.visual_prompt: Split-screen: modern grocery shelf with dated products on one side, ancient Egyptian tomb cross-section on the other

scenes.line: Here's why: honey has almost zero water. Bacteria cannot survive in it.
scenes.visual_prompt: Microscopic view of crystalline honey structure, magnified crystals catching light, molecular simplicity visualized

scenes.line: It's so antimicrobial that Egyptians actually used it to mummify bodies.
scenes.visual_prompt: Silhouette of wrapped mummy figure against warm golden light, suggesting preservation and timelessness

scenes.line: A sealed jar of honey will outlive you, your kids, and their kids.
scenes.visual_prompt: Single golden honey jar on dark shelf, dust particles floating in warm light around it, suggesting infinite time passing

scenes.line: The only enemy of honey? Heat and moisture breaking the seal.
scenes.visual_prompt: Honey jar with broken wax seal, moisture droplets forming on glass, warm glow suggesting exposure

cta: If you could keep one food fresh forever, would you choose honey or something completely different?
